passage:
Kashish, I saw your light on at three again. Let me tell you about your Dilnaz Phuppo at sixteen. For five weeks before my board exams I did nothing but draw in the margins and listen to the radio. Then one Sunday, panic. I sat from six in the morning till past eight at night with history, geography, civics, all of it, living on tea. I felt like a warrior. I told everyone.
My Ammi watched and said nothing, only brought more tea. On Monday I couldn't open a book. Tuesday either. My eyes burned and the dates slid right off my brain. Ammi said, "A river doesn't fill in one day." I lost that whole week to headaches and sulking.
In the exam I remembered every detail of the Mughals, which I'd done first that Sunday, and almost nothing about rivers, which I'd done at seven in the evening, half asleep. The paper had two long questions on rivers.

qa.q: Which topic did Dilnaz remember best in the exam?
qa.a: Every detail of the Mughals, which were done first that Sunday.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz feel during the long Sunday, and afterwards?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt heroic, like a warrior, on Sunday, then drained and sulky, unable to open a book on Monday or Tuesday.

qa.q: Which choice in the story set up the collapse, and what might have worked instead?
qa.a: Doing nothing for five weeks and cramming it all into one Sunday; a couple of steady hours each day would have covered rivers as well as the Mughals.

qa.q: How might Ammi have seen the big Sunday?
qa.a: Ammi seems to have seen it as something that could not last, quietly bringing tea and then saying on Monday that a river doesn't fill in one day.

grounding: Shows a teenager cramming for a whole day after weeks of nothing, then burning out for a week with patchy knowledge.

passage:
On the first of January, Rashmi taped a chart to the wall of her room in Palampur: run to the tea gardens at five, fifty push-ups, one hour of English, no sweets. She drew thirty boxes for the month.
For five days she ticked every box, breath steaming in the cold, and showed her sister Jyoti the chart each night.
On the sixth day, her cousin's wedding ran till two in the morning. She slept through the alarm, ate three laddoos at breakfast, and stared at the empty box.
"That's it. It's ruined," she said.
"It's one day," said Jyoti.
"The chart's spoiled now." Rashmi took it down and folded it into a drawer. She didn't run on the seventh day, or the eighth. By the end of January the English book had a layer of dust on it, and the chart was still in the drawer, with five ticks.

qa.q: For how many days did Rashmi tick every box?
qa.a: For five days she ticked every box.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling when she said "It's ruined"?
qa.a: Rashmi felt disappointed and defeated, seeing one missed day as spoiling the whole chart.

qa.q: What could Rashmi try after a missed day like the wedding?
qa.a: Rashmi could just pick up the next day, even with a shorter run or half an hour of English, instead of treating one gap as the end.

qa.q: How does Jyoti see the missed day?
qa.a: Jyoti sees it as just one day, not a reason to stop, which is why Jyoti says, "It's one day."

grounding: Shows a young adult starting an ambitious routine with energy and abandoning all of it after the first missed day.

passage:
"You're making a calendar for the whole semester?" Nirmala leaned over Tenzin's desk.
"Just the shape of it. These three weeks in November are exams, so they're red. I'll study most of the day then. No football, no trips home."
"And after?"
"That week in green is the easy week. Sleep, football, call Amala, go home to Darjeeling. And the grey weeks before are normal: classes, two hours of revision a day."
"Last year you just went red from August."
"I know. By the exams I couldn't read a page without my eyes closing. And I fell sick right after."
"So red is allowed now?"
"Red is allowed if green comes after. The exams need the push. I just can't live in it."
Nirmala picked up a pen. "Make me one. My project deadline falls in the same week."
Tenzin grinned and pulled out another sheet. "Red, then green. Promise you'll actually take the green."

qa.q: Which weeks does Tenzin mark in red?
qa.a: The three weeks in November, when the exams are.

qa.q: Why did Nirmala ask Tenzin to make one too?
qa.a: Nirmala seems persuaded and hopeful, and perhaps a little worried, since a project deadline falls in the same week and the plan looks like it could help.

qa.q: What makes Tenzin's plan more sustainable than last year's?
qa.a: Tenzin allows an intense red phase only for the exams and plans a green week of rest right after, instead of sprinting from August.

qa.q: What would change if Tenzin skipped the green week again?
qa.a: Tenzin could end up exhausted and sick after the exams, just like last year.

grounding: Shows a student accepting an intense exam phase but planning easier weeks and rest around it.

"Wait, you drew this?" Chinmay held up Shankar's tablet. "The hands are actually right."
"Took a year," Shankar said. "Thirty minutes every morning before work. Hands, mostly."
"We started the same week! I did those eight-hour Sundays."
"I remember. You were better than me in March."
"Then I got busy. Missed a few Sundays, and when I came back I'd forgotten everything." Chinmay scrolled. "Did you ever feel like quitting?"
"All summer. Four months and my drawings looked exactly the same. I nearly deleted the app."
"Why didn't you?"
"I made it too small to skip. Thirty minutes, one page. Even on bad days. Around October something clicked, and it's been getting faster since."
Chinmay put the tablet down. "Thirty minutes. That's less than my commute."
"That's the trick. Want to start tomorrow? I'll send you my hand pages from week one. They're awful."

qa.q: How long did Shankar practise each morning?
qa.a: Thirty minutes every morning before work.

qa.q: What was Shankar feeling during the summer?
qa.a: Shankar felt discouraged and close to quitting, because four months of drawing looked exactly the same.

qa.q: What kept Shankar going when the results didn't show?
qa.a: Making the habit too small to skip: thirty minutes and one page, even on bad days.

qa.q: How does Chinmay feel on seeing Shankar's drawing?
qa.a: Chinmay is surprised and a little envious, since they started the same week and Chinmay was ahead in March.

grounding: Shows a steady worker's short daily practice pulling far ahead of occasional binges after a long stretch of invisible progress.

subtype: Colleague who is reliable rather than brilliant [Observer]
passage:
Week one. Aditi, new to the editing team, assumed Mehul was the one to watch. At the Monday meeting he pitched three dazzling story ideas. Vaibhav, in the corner, only said, "I'll have the two city pieces by Thursday." Aditi barely noticed him.
Week four. Mehul hadn't filed in eleven days and wasn't answering calls. On Thursday, as on every Thursday, Vaibhav's two pieces arrived before lunch, clean, captions checked. When the chief editor needed someone for a tight results page, Aditi watched her skip Mehul's name and say, "Vaibhav, can you?"
Week ten. Mehul reappeared with a brilliant long feature, and everyone praised it. But at the planning meeting, when a new beat opened, the whole table looked at Vaibhav. Aditi noticed she had started doing the same: whenever she needed something certain, she walked over to his corner.

qa.q: When did Vaibhav's two pieces arrive in week four?
qa.a: On Thursday, before lunch, clean with captions checked.

qa.q: How did Aditi's feelings about Vaibhav change over the weeks?
qa.a: Aditi was at first impressed by Mehul and barely noticed Vaibhav, but came to trust Vaibhav, walking over whenever she needed something certain.

qa.q: What could Mehul take from how the team treats Vaibhav?
qa.a: Mehul could see that steady, on-time filing earns trust, and could commit to smaller pieces he can deliver every week.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav experience the whole table looking at him for the new beat?
qa.a: Vaibhav might feel quietly valued, seeing that weeks of steady work have earned more trust than occasional brilliance.

grounding: Shows a team coming to trust the quiet colleague who delivers every week more than the star who vanishes and reappears.

passage:
Hrithik, you asked how I kept up my riyaz all those years. When I, Kamal, was twenty-five and working at the railway office in Jhansi, my guruji gave me one rule. "Miss a day if you must. Never miss two."
I thought it sounded too easy. Then came the winter I had a bad fever and could barely sit up. On the second day I asked my wife to bring the sitar to the bed, and I played one scale, slowly, for five minutes. My fingers shook. But the chain was alive.
Guruji called that the floor. On good days, an hour. On train journeys, I tapped the fingering on my knee for ten minutes. On fever days, one scale. Never zero twice.
Forty years later I still play every morning. Not because I'm strong, beta. Because the floor was low enough to step over even on my worst day.

qa.q: What rule did guruji give Kamal?
qa.a: "Miss a day if you must. Never miss two."

qa.q: What did Kamal first feel about guruji's rule?
qa.a: Kamal was doubtful and a little dismissive, thinking it sounded too easy to matter.

qa.q: Which choice during the fever kept Kamal's habit alive?
qa.a: On the second day of the fever Kamal played one slow scale for five minutes from bed, so two days were never missed.

qa.q: How might Kamal's wife have seen the request for the sitar in bed?
qa.a: Kamal's wife was probably worried but also touched by that determination, bringing the sitar for a five-minute scale.

grounding: Shows a habit-builder allowing a missed day but never two in a row, keeping a minimum version for bad days.

passage:
In her Hyderabad flat, Sangeeta had moved her alarm to five and her bedtime to past two. The entrance exam was in March; every hour felt like marks. She ate lunch with one hand and held a physics book in the other, and she dropped the evening walk with Afreen.
By the third week things started slipping. In the coaching test she read a question about a pulley three times and still couldn't hold it in her head. She blanked on a formula she had known since class nine. On the bus she dozed off and missed her stop.
"You look like a ghost," Afreen said on the phone.
"I'm fine. I'm just putting in more hours than everyone."
Her test score came back lower than the month before. Sangeeta stared at it, then at the timetable on her wall, where the word "sleep" had been crossed out in red.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta miss when she dozed off on the bus?
qa.a: She missed her stop.

qa.q: Why did Sangeeta insist "I'm fine" to Afreen?
qa.a: Sangeeta felt proud of the extra hours and anxious about the exam, so she saw her tiredness as a worthy sacrifice rather than a warning.

qa.q: What small change could help Sangeeta's scores?
qa.a: Putting sleep back on the timetable and keeping the evening walk, so her concentration and memory recover enough to use the hours she studies.

qa.q: How does Afreen see what is happening?
qa.a: Afreen sees that Sangeeta is worn out, saying she looks like a ghost, and is probably worried about her.

grounding: Shows a teenager cutting sleep and breaks for a competitive exam and finding concentration and memory falling.

passage:
Wei used to love the Tuesday robotics club at her university in Melbourne. This term she stopped going. "What's the point," she told Tariq. "We build a robot, it breaks, we build another."
She slept ten hours on Saturday and still woke with heavy arms. Her scholarship essays, her tutoring shifts, her lab reports and the weekly call home to her parents, who kept saying how proud they were, all sat on her list like bricks. She felt guilty for not feeling grateful.
On Thursday Tariq found her in the library staring at a blank screen. "You've been saying 'whatever' about everything for a month," he said. "That's not you."
Wei rubbed her eyes. "Maybe I'm just lazy."
"Lazy people don't do four jobs," Tariq said. "Let's look at the list together, and maybe book the student support office."
She didn't answer, but she didn't close the laptop either.

qa.q: Which club did Wei stop going to?
qa.a: The Tuesday robotics club.

qa.q: Why did Wei feel guilty?
qa.a: Wei felt guilty for not feeling grateful, since her parents kept saying how proud they were while her tasks felt like bricks.

qa.q: What sensible step did Tariq suggest?
qa.a: Looking at the list together to see what could ease, and booking the student support office.

qa.q: How does Tariq see Wei's tiredness?
qa.a: Tariq sees it as a sign of too much load, not laziness, telling her that lazy people don't do four jobs.

grounding: Shows a student becoming cynical, tired despite rest and less caring, as signs of an unsustainable load rather than weakness.

passage:
Dear Ramesh,
You asked why I've gone quiet on our group chat. Honestly, work has eaten the evenings. Nobody ever told me to reply at night. It started with the team lead sending a message at eleven, "no rush", and someone answering in two minutes. Then everyone did. Then the Sunday messages began, always friendly, always "when you get a chance".
Now I sleep with the phone under my pillow. I check it before brushing my teeth. Last Saturday I was at my niece's birthday and answered four messages during the cake.
The strange part is that I used to love this job. I read design blogs for fun. I haven't opened one since June. I feel tired in a way weekends don't fix.
I'm thinking of setting my status to "offline after 8" and seeing who objects. Tell me if that sounds mad.
Kavitha

qa.q: When did the team lead send the first late message?
qa.a: At eleven, saying "no rush".

qa.q: How does Kavitha feel about the job now compared with before?
qa.a: Kavitha feels worn out and has lost interest, having once loved the job and read design blogs for fun but not opened one since June.

qa.q: What small step is Kavitha considering, and what might help it work?
qa.a: Setting a status of "offline after 8"; saying so openly to the team and sticking to it would bring the unspoken rule into the open.

qa.q: What would change if the team lead said clearly that night messages can wait till morning?
qa.a: The unspoken pressure to answer in two minutes might ease, and people like Kavitha could rest without the phone under the pillow.

grounding: Shows an employee gradually losing rest and interest through unspoken expectations to reply late at night and at weekends.

passage:
I sit across from Bhupen in the accounts section, and something changed around the end of the quarter. He used to hum while he worked. Then he stopped. He snapped at the office assistant over sugar in his tea, which I had never seen. He sent the vendor file with last month's figures, twice. At lunch he took his box to his desk instead of the canteen.
In the Monday meeting our manager said, "Bhupen, sleeping on the job?" and a couple of people laughed. Bhupen went red and said nothing.
I didn't know what was going on inside him, and I still don't fully. But that evening I waited till the floor emptied and said, "You've seemed really tired lately. No pressure, but I'm around if you want to talk." He was silent, then said he hadn't slept properly in weeks. I mentioned our company's counselling line and wrote the number on a sticky note. He tucked it into his wallet.
I'm Gautam, by the way. I just thought someone should ask.

qa.q: What did Bhupen send twice?
qa.a: The vendor file with last month's figures.

qa.q: What might Gautam have been feeling while watching the Monday meeting?
qa.a: Gautam was probably uncomfortable and concerned, seeing Bhupen go red while others laughed, and that led to the private check-in that evening.

qa.q: Why did Gautam's check-in work better than the manager's remark?
qa.a: It was private and caring, naming tiredness without blame and offering the counselling line, while the public joke only embarrassed Bhupen.

qa.q: What was the Monday meeting like for Bhupen?
qa.a: It was probably humiliating for Bhupen, who went red and said nothing while people laughed.

grounding: Shows a coworker noticing irritability, careless errors and withdrawal, and choosing a private, caring check-in that points to professional help.
